target.title: The panic was a story about a story

content.text:
The panic was a story about a story.

In 1938 Orson Welles read War of the Worlds on the radio. America supposedly lost its mind. It did not. The audience was small.

Newspapers were losing ad money to radio and had every reason to make radio look dangerous.

So they wrote the panic.

Halloween was never about fear.

It grew out of Samhain, the Gaelic festival marking the end of harvest and the start of winter, when the boundary between this world and the next was believed to thin.

It was about the year turning, and needing a ritual for the dark half of it.

They put a stone in the child's mouth.

A Roman era grave excavated at Lugnano in Italy held a stone placed deliberately, one of a set of burials archaeologists read as meant to stop the dead returning.

Every generation does something physical about a fear it cannot argue with. Ours is just quieter.

She was 18.

Mary Shelley started Frankenstein in the summer of 1816, the year without a summer. Ash from Tambora, a volcano on the other side of the world, kept Europe under cloud and the group at the lake indoors.

Bad weather, nowhere to go, nothing going right. She invented a genre anyway.

The conditions were never the requirement.
